Peter Andre, Richard Wilkins and Kate Ceberano share memories of ‘a truly unique character’ and ‘the fan all artists wish to have’
Molly Meldrum, Countdown host and promoter of Australian music, dies aged 83
Friends and fans of Molly Meldrum have remembered the music industry great, who died on Monday at the age of 83 .
Meldrum spent more than a decade hosting the ABC music show Countdown, leaving a lasting legacy on the Australian music landscape.
Anthony Albanese was among those paying tribute. “With an interview style that was inimitable and an enthusiasm that was uncontainable, Molly Meldrum loved music almost as much as we loved him,” the wrote in a post on X.
“On Countdown and beyond, he championed Australian artists and brought international acts to our shores. He gave new artists a leg up and established artists a welcoming embrace. And over the years as he implored us to do ourselves a favour, he became a central part of the Australian soundtrack. We were lucky to have him. May Ian ‘Molly’ Meldrum rest in peace.”
Jason Donovan said Meldrum was the “very heart” of the music program while he was growing up, calling the man a “truly unique character, a great Australian and one of this country’s greatest pioneers and ambassadors for music and entertainment”.
“He was loved, recognised and respected around the world for the extraordinary contribution he made to Australian music and the artists he championed,” Donovan wrote on Facebook. “There will never be another quite like him.”
The former Neighbours star shared a memory of Meldrum appearing on an episode alongside Kylie Minogue and Guy Pearce, adding: “What a day that was!”
On Instagram, US band Blondie acknowledged the role Meldrum played in their reach. “Molly was instrumental in Blondie’s success in Australia, championing our music and introducing us to a whole new audience. We will always be grateful for his belief in us and the doors he helped open. He had a true passion for music, a wonderful sense of humor, and was truly one of a kind. He will be greatly missed.”
The television presenter Richard Wilkins remembered his longtime friend on-air on Monday morning. The pair used to travel around the world for interviews, Wilkins said, which led to great memories and hilarious stories.
“Australian music would not be Australian music without Molly’s incredible contribution,” Wilkins said. “I shared so many overseas trips with Molly, which was a joy and a curse. He lost 13 passports, that was the tally I got to.
“We went from a Michael Jackson gig in Munich to see Bruce Springsteen in Paris. That was the sort of thing we used to get up to back in the day.”
On Facebook, UK singer Leo Sayer praised the “wonderful, fun, crazy, knowledgeable, influential and irrepressible soul who will live on in all our memories as long as rock‘n’roll will … Ian introduced me to the Australian scene back in 1974 when I first appeared on ABC’s Countdown TV and was a huge part of my success down under.”
Gavin Wood, a longtime friend of Meldrum’s who worked on Countdown, said the host was “one of the craziest, most colourful, funniest and most beautiful people you could ever have the pleasure of meeting”.
“What he has done for the Australian music industry is simply phenomenal,” Wood wrote . “His contribution, passion, enthusiasm and unwavering commitment to Australian artists helped shape an entire generation of music and entertainment.
“There will never be another Molly Meldrum. You simply cannot measure anyone against him.”
Meldrum produced Russell Morris’s 1969 single the Real Thing, which reached #1 on the charts. “He was a unique, and loveable individual,” Morris wrote on Facebook . “I was lucky enough to call him my friend, and mentor. The journey we went on was pretty surreal – his creative energy and insights were exceptional … He achieved things that were truly great. Things that sometimes seemed impossible.”
“He was such a huge presence in the Australian music industry and was a great friend and supporter of so many up and coming bands and artists – ourselves included,” the band Human Nature wrote . “Thanks for everything Molly. Rest easy.”
The singer Peter Andre posted a photo with Meldrum, praising him for helping to elevate his career and saying “this really hurts”.
“If it wasn’t for this man, I would not of had any of the chances I had to make it in any way in the entertainment industry back when it was near impossible to get noticed,” Andre wrote . “He believed in me from day one and I am forever grateful to Ian ‘Molly’ Meldrum.”
Kate Ceberano wrote: “He had no agenda he wanted, no praise, he never basked in any reflected glory or self pride. He simply wanted the world to hear what he could hear, wanted you to see what he was looking at and then blow it up to 11. Way up sky high. No dream is too big. No cringe, withholding nothing.
Iva Davies of Icehouse also paid tribute : “He was such a bright, larger than life figure in our Australian music scene for so many years … Like the rest of the music community that owed so much to his support, the band and I are so thankful that Molly was a part of our lives and music. There will never be another like him and he will be sorely missed by so many.”
In an interview with 2GB, Marcia Hines said: “I considered Molly a friend, a dear, dear friend, and an advocate for our music … He believed in us. That’s what he did for us. He believed in all of us … We’ve lost such an incredible person in our industry.”
She continued: “What you saw was what you got. That was really Molly. He fumbled. He laughed. He laughed at himself. But most importantly he loved us.”
The Australian Recording Industry Association issued its own praise of Meldrum’s work, noting that both he and the Countdown program were the first inductees into the Aria Hall of Fame who weren’t recording artists, back in 2014.
“It is impossible to imagine what Australian music would look like without Molly’s long and storied career,” said Annabelle Herd, Aria’s chief executive. “He shaped the music taste of a generation of Australians and gave so much of himself for the good of Australian artists, for which our whole industry is eternally grateful.”
The St Kilda football club remembered Meldrum as a “lifelong Sainter”, saying the organisation was deeply saddened by his death.
“An iconic and passionate supporter of our football club, Molly changed and brightened the lives of so many across a storied career,” the club wrote on Facebook .

You can personalize the SlideTag with a photo slideshow, message, or QR code transferred from your phone over Bluetooth.
After expanding its Charmera collection with a Millennium Edition featuring Y2K-inspired designs earlier this year, Reto’s follow-up to its tiny Kodak camera is an equally small digital photo frame you can use to display your shots. But while the Charmera’s usefulness stopped at snapping grainy photos and terrible videos , the Kodak SlideTag goes one step further. It also functions as a Bluetooth tracker that’s compatible with either Apple’s Find My or Google’s Find Hub tracking networks.
The Kodak SlideTag will be available for $34.99 each and, like the Charmera, will feature a series of retro designs distributed in mystery boxes so you don’t know which one you’re going to get. Kodak also sells a complete set of all eight vintage designs for $279.92 if you don’t like mysteries; however, there’s a ninth “secret edition” only available in the individual boxes with a sleek metallic finish.
For those who grew up in an era where projectors are small enough to integrate into phones , the SlideTag is designed to look like a modernized version of the film slides that were used to project photos decades ago. Instead of film, the SlideTag features a 1.54-inch color E Ink screen that mixes six colored inks to display photos at a resolution of 240 x 240.
The color reproduction won’t be as accurate as an LCD or OLED screen, but the SlideTag can hold and cycle up to 12 photos transferred to the device over Bluetooth from Kodak’s Memory Link app running on a mobile device. You can also use it to display a short to-do list, contact details, a countdown timer, or a QR code linking to wherever you want.
As a tracker it’s not quite as functional as an Apple AirTag or Google’s Pixel Tag , which use features like ultra wideband (UWB) and Channel Sounding to make them easier to find. The SlideTag sticks to basic Bluetooth with a range of up to 30 meters out in the open and a 75-decibel buzzer to help locate it when you’re close. Battery life will vary depending on how frequently you use tracking features or refresh the displayed image, but the SlideTag uses a common CR2032 coin cell battery that’s easy to replace.

When Notable Capital poured roughly 10% of the U.S. portion of its $1 billion-plus fund into Anthropic’s Series E, many limited partners were perplexed by the massive bet. Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threatening to overtake closed-source competitors. Moreover, at $61.5 billion, Anthropic’s valuation was by far the highest that the predominantly early-stage venture firm had invested at in its 25-year history.
But investors at Notable, formerly known as GGV Capital before its 2024 split from its China operations, were confident in Anthropic’s future. A team that included managing partners Hans Tung and Glenn Solomon and principal Dan Cahana crunched the numbers and found that developers were increasingly favoring Claude over ChatGPT, using Claude 70% of the time, a reversal from the previous year.
“We just knew that for AI, the developer is at the center because they’re the early adopters,” Tung, a co-founder of the firm, told TechCrunch.
Having navigated the complexities of U.S.-China relations firsthand, Notable was also convinced that “mission-critical” work would always require U.S.-based, closed-source models, Tung said.
Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment. On Wednesday, Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times.
Notable is, of course, not the only firm sitting on a massive paper windfall from Anthropic. Even traditional late-stage investors, who rarely see venture-scale multiples, are set for a big win.
Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC had been researching Anthropic throughout 2024, but it didn’t make its first investment until after Chris Emanuel, head of the fund’s tech investments, met with Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao at Che Fico, an Italian restaurant in San Francisco, in early 2025. Rao helped pique Emanuel’s interest in the company by showing that model improvements were driving rising enterprise adoption. GIC then made its first investment in Anthropic’s Series F, a round announced in September 2025 at a $183 billion valuation.
“Claude Code was just released then,” Emanuel told TechCrunch. “It was very early, but even then, we could see signs that it was really popular with developers.” GIC’s conviction in the AI lab was so high that the fund later led Anthropic’s Series G alongside Coatue at a $380 billion valuation, and returned as one of the co-leads for the pre-IPO round at $965 billion. Across the three rounds, GIC invested more than $4.5 billion in Anthropic, amassing a stake equal to about 1% of the company after its IPO, according to a person familiar with GIC’s financials.
Lilian Li, who leads U.S. growth investments at Baillie Gifford, began studying Anthropic and speaking with its team nearly two years before first investing in the company’s Series F. Baillie Gifford invested in the Claude maker once it became clear that the company was “executing consistently” on its vision while generating strong revenue and “compelling gross margins,” Li told TechCrunch.
After Baillie Gifford’s initial investment, Anthropic continued to deliver on its promises, expanding into industries such as legal services and life sciences, as well as broader applications like Cowork and cybersecurity, Li said.
“It’s actually quite incredible how consistent they have been with how quickly everything’s been changing,” she added. Baillie Gifford went on to invest a total of $1.5 billion across three funding rounds, a bet that has generated substantial paper gains for the investment manager, as well as for dozens of other backers who invested at what once seemed like astronomical valuations.

Microsoft and the US government agree there are more outages to come.
Over the last week or so, we have seen a nationwide FAA ground stop, a multi-day Outlook outage that brought entire companies to a standstill, and a banking outage at JPMorgan Chase . But the consensus is that there are more to come . Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN :
“The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.”
Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning about further outages on CBS News’ Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan , but sounded a much more ominous tone.
“I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn’t the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks … The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now.”
While the outages over the last week were not believed to be caused by cyberattacks, Smith said that AI has made it easier to find flaws , “and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems,” he said.
The last few months have also seen an increase in attacks on government and commercial systems, including those at the USDA , JP Morgan , and supermarkets .
Whether outages are brought on by AI-assisted hackers or human error during the rush to patch an aging system , one thing seems certain: there will be more in the coming months.
Update November 22nd: Added clarification that Smith was speaking on Face the Nation, not to CBS generally. Due to a typo, this article originally stated that the outages were believed to be caused by cyberattacks, the missing word has been corrected.

A new blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity.
Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.”
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.”
But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name ) could be that measurement.
In Pachochki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.”
Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5.
“GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.”
So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.”

John Kennedy looks to Trump leaders as he asks how China evidently bypassed export controls for Nvidia’s top AI chips
Invoking Greek mythology, US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang ’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”.
The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday. Host Kristen Welker asked Kennedy, known for his colloquialisms, if US national security was put at risk by Huang’s affair, given the position his company’s chips have occupied at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom.
Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on 12 November after allegations surfaced of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been executive director of Megaspeed International. Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of export controls in the US, where the Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced AI chips to China.
On Sunday’s edition of CNN’s State of the Union , the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton, said he suspected China was able to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips.
He also said on Fox News Sunday: “There are chips that have ended up in places that they should not.”
Kennedy said he was “less interested in … what [Huang] did” than in asking the Trump administration’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick , and its treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, about how China was evidently able to circumvent US “export controls”.
“Mr Huang … did what he did. I hope he had a good time. It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy,” Kennedy said.
Lutnick has faced scrutiny over allegedly ignoring warnings that Megaspeed was smuggling chips to China. Other administration leaders, including Bessent, wanted to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist – but the commerce department stalled enforcement of it.
Kennedy said he could only conclude commerce department leaders are either “so incompetent you wouldn’t put them in charge of a food truck” – or “they knowingly allowed this to happen”.
He said he wanted to get Bessent and Lutnick under oath in front of a Senate committee to “answer some hard questions”.
“And if secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” Kennedy said.
Bessent said on Sunday’s edition of CBS News’s Face the Nation that the Trump administration had been in touch with Nvidia’s temporary management, lead directors and lawyers while trying to find out who was in charge of compliance at the company.
“It behooves Nvidia to move ⁠quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Bessent said on the program.
Kennedy, a former Louisiana state treasurer who began his political career as a Democrat before switching parties and becoming a staunch Trump administration ally, delivers many of the colloquialisms that have become his calling card with a southern US drawl.
Many believe Kennedy resorts to the drawl to come off as folksy – while he holds degrees from Vanderbilt University, the University of Virginia School of Law and the UK’s Oxford University, and is estimated to be one of the wealthiest US senators.

In recent years, people have been increasingly looking for new ways to form platonic connections, as loneliness and social isolation have become more prevalent.

The service charges a $22.22 curation fee or a monthly subscription for the same price.

Transparency International says Queensland’s David Crisafulli was ‘by far the most frequently accessed’ state leader, with 13 meetings
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Bosses at 10 datacentre companies secured almost 120 meetings with premiers and ministers in five states over a three-year period, with experts declaring this is “just the tip of the iceberg”.
Analysis by Transparency International Australia argues these meetings, when combined with political donations, demonstrate “unfettered access” to decision-makers that creates an “uneven playing field”.
The report found donations from major datacentre companies and their contracted lobbying firms nearly tripled over the past three years from $685,000 to $1.8m, coinciding with increased investment across Australia.
The analysis found the Queensland leader, David Crisafulli , was “by far the most frequently accessed state premier”, with public diaries showing he has met datacentre executives 13 times in the past three years.
This included three meetings in as many weeks in August and September with Australia’s largest datacentre operator, NextDC – roughly one month before the company’s expansion in Melbourne was halted after its power provider delayed construction of new power poles due to community backlash .
“Those meetings took place shortly before the Queensland premier announced a dedicated framework to fast-track datacentre approvals by taking them out of the hands of local councils,” the Transparency International report said.
Crisafulli has embraced datacentre investment and flew to the United States in September to secure a $31.9bn deal with the AI giant Anthropic for what could become Australia’s largest datacentre . His office was contacted for comment.
During this three-year period, 119 meetings with ministers or premiers were held in New South Wales , Victoria, Tasmania, Queensland and the ACT. These are the only jurisdictions to publicly release ministerial diaries. The meetings were mostly held in 2026.
“These numbers are just the tip of the iceberg,” said Clancy Moore, the chief executive of Transparency International Australia.
“What we don’t know is how many meetings companies like NextDC, OpenAI and Anthropic and their third-party lobbyists are having with the prime minister and ministers in our federal parliament.
“Australia’s lobbying laws also don’t cover in-house lobbyists or government relations staff so there’s very little oversight of their activities too.”
The report also found Australian company Firmus Technologies secured 10 meetings with Tasmanian ministers and the premier this year alone. During this period, the company’s expansion in the state has faced sustained backlash from local communities who feel they were not properly consulted .
The three companies that secured the most meetings with ministers were Amazon Web Services, Macquarie Technology Group and NextDC.
Last month, Guardian Australia reported on political donations from Amazon and Macquarie to both major parties, closely aligning with the announcement of multimillion-dollar government contracts or planning developments. Both companies say these donations were not aimed at influencing policy and that their timing was coincidental.
A shareholder at NextDC’s annual general meeting on Friday said the company had “a lot of lobbying going on in Canberra” but called on the company to better lobby the public on the benefits of datacentres.
The company’s chair, Stephen Flynn, said he was “not sure we are great at lobbying as an industry or as a company” but the world had now changed.
“We thought we were just going along and [being] invisible, in the way if you think about all telecommunications systems … [it] is kind of invisible. We just take it for granted. But we can’t do that. We can’t do that as we go forward.”
The report has also cited examples of four senior public servants at federal government departments quitting to assume leadership positions at OpenAI, AirTrunk and CDC. Three of these appointments were made this year.
In September, the president of the Australian Professional Government Relations Association, Sally Mackenzie, said the scale of engagement between industry and ministers was a sign of the system working as intended.
“What we’re seeing with AI and datacentres is that dynamic playing out at real pace, because the stakes for industry, government and Australians more broadly are so high,” Mackenzie said.
“Lobbying is an important part of the democratic process. It ensures that all stakeholders have the ability to communicate with government.”

Major delays for Delta come just a week after a nationwide groundstop.
All Delta flights in and out of Atlanta are facing significant delays on Sunday due to a problem with the system that calculates a plane’s weight and balance. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is Delta’s largest hub and one of the busiest airports in the world. While only Delta is impacted at the moment, disruptions at Hartsfield-Jackson could potentially affect other airports and airlines if delays continue to pile up.
The issues with Delta’s systems in Atlanta come just one week after an FAA outage led to a nationwide groundstop and thousands of canceled flights. According to The New York Times :
The system that went offline calculates the total weight of an airplane, including its airframe, fuel, passengers and their baggage. The system also allows pilots to determine the plane’s center of gravity and whether the weight is evenly distributed — data points that help ensure safe passage.
“Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” the airline said in a statement on Sunday.

In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.
The book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections . And those debates are likely to continue as Democrats wield more governmental power .
In an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry. After all, if a data center is being built in your community, “it’s very physical, it’s very material.”
“It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on,“ Marx said. “You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.”
He also suggested that data center opposition is only the most visible piece of a wider movement targeting “the physical manifestations of the tech industry, […] whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.”
During our conversation (which I’ve edited for length and clarity), Marx and I discussed data centers’ environmental impact, how tech companies are responding to community resistance, and what it’s actually like inside a data center.
I liked your description of trying to get access to the inside of a “hyperscale” data center and then eventually taking a tour [of one]. Could you talk a little bit more about what that experience was like? How did you get in? What surprised you when you actually got in?
Getting inside of a hyperscale data center was not the easiest task in the world. I spoke to some researchers who have been doing research on data centers for a number of years longer than I had, and they told me that before the generative AI moment, and before all the attention that has been put on data centers recently, that it was quite a bit easier to do so.
I sent emails to a number of companies asking if I could get inside, often didn’t get a response, other times got a no. I ended up, after visiting the outsides of some data centers in places like northern Virginia and Ireland and spots like that, I actually went down to New Zealand to go inside of a data center itself. And the thing that struck me most was the level of security.
Obviously, you would expect that this is an infrastructure that is really securitized, because the data inside needs to be kept safe, obviously [they] have these big fences and all the security cameras around the data centers. But to go inside, I had to send my passport in advance. Then when I got there, they had to check the passport, and then as we were going through the data center itself, every single door in the data center was locked unless you had a key card to unlock it.
Then, when you get inside of the server room itself, where all this computer hardware is stored in tall racks that look like cabinets — you can imagine, in your mind, that this would be kind of a sinister location, with some eerie lighting or something like that. But in truth, it’s just quite utilitarian. It’s a warm room with some air conditioning blasting into the servers from vents that are nearby.
It was really loud as well, because you have all these fans running from all these servers, it was really kind of piercing. To be inside of this room, if you were going to be in there for a while, you’d probably want earplugs or something like that.
Before I read your book, I thought of data centers as something that’s important, but a little bit boring. How did you decide they were interesting and rich enough to sustain an entire book?
I felt the same. I was aware that data centers had been out there, but it was not something that I was paying particularly close attention to. But then there were a number of stories that of tipped me off to the fact that there might be more here, and that it was worth looking deeper into what was going on — the first being hearing about the water pressures created by data centers in Chile around the capital of Santiago , where companies like Google and Microsoft were building data centers, and communities were concerned about their access to water and started organizing around that.
And then hearing about how much electricity data centers were consuming in Ireland, to the point that now they consume more than 20% of the country’s electricity , and that was obviously pushing up power prices. It was putting pressures on the grid, such that the grid operator actually put a moratorium in place for grid connections for data centers around the Dublin area, back in 2022. This was even before the generative AI moment that caused a surge in construction of data centers.
And then the other one was in The Dalles, Oregon, where Google had actually built its first company-owned data centers about 20 years back. In that case, its water deal was coming up for renewal. It wanted to build more data centers there, so it needed more water. And when the residents started asking, “How much water is Google actually using?” a journalist at The Oregonian went to the city and essentially asked, “Hey, how much water is Google using? Our readers would like to know this,” he was hit with a lawsuit instead of being given that information. Because Google did not want it to be public. And then, of course, when it did come out about a year later, Google revealed that it was using 29% of the city’s water, which seemed quite significant.
That was around when ChatGPT was being released and generative AI was starting to take off. It felt like, okay, there are these pockets of places where a lot of data centers have already been constructed, where they are putting pressures on the communities that are causing people to respond, and it felt like that was going to start coming to a lot more communities. It was a good time to really start to dig in and pay attention.
You don’t just talk about the data centers’ environmental impact, but also, they [become] your way in to talk about this broader tech moment. They represent to you — particularly the hyperscale data centers — represent to you how these tech companies are doing business now.
Absolutely. The hyperscale data centers and just the scale of the construction — whether it’s the the size of the actual facilities themselves or the number that these companies are trying to build out, just feels fundamentally unsustainable.
They’re just demanding too much from the communities where they’re being located, whether that’s because of electricity or because of water use or what have you, or just the fact that they’re building out so many, that when you think about the cumulative impact and you look at the demand for water, but particularly for energy from fossil fuels, that means that it’s just completely out of line with a livable planet and an amount of computation that feels like it makes any degree of sense for us to have constructed.
I think it really goes back to the hubris of the tech industry and of these major tech companies and the tech billionaires that run them, and the fact that they have these particular visions of the future that are based on fantasies , but also on expanding their own power and influence over the world, and they don’t seem to mind that everyone else then has to pay the cost that comes with their ambitions and what they are seeking to do.
And I feel like it’s become particularly egregious wit…

Waymo pulling its robotaxis off freeways (again) and Zoox robotaxis launching on the Uber app illustrate the push and pull between progress and setbacks in the autonomous vehicle industry.
There are signs of growth. For instance, Tesla has now surpassed Waymo in Texas in the number of robotaxis registered with the state (Tesla has 1,507 and Waymo has 1,345). But does that translate to market dominance?
A better metric, if we’re trying to gauge who is leading, would be commercial driverless miles. And if we’re measuring cost-efficiency, another useful metric would be driverless miles per vehicle. By those measures, Waymo is still ahead, based on data available to me. But with Waymo’s recent freeways setback and Tesla’s push to expand its robotaxi fleet with Cybercabs, that lead could shrink.
Not that there needs to be a winner, by the way. Transportation is deeply fragmented, and there is room for multiple players in the U.S., not to mention the rest of the world.
A recent discussion with my Autonocast co-host Ed Niedermeyer, whose book, “Elon Take the Wheel,” comes out December 1, got me thinking about how Las Vegas could soon become a real world A/B test of sorts for human-driven vs. autonomous ride-hailing services.
Uber, as mentioned above, just added Zoox to its ride-hailing app in Las Vegas. For now, riders don’t have much of a choice. Uber customers can increase their chances of getting a Zoox robotaxi, and they can always decline a robot ride. But they can’t directly select a robotaxi. Instead, Uber riders will be matched with one if it’s available.
Uber said that will soon change. The company plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in its app as “availability and reliability improve,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in November.
Las Vegas will also become the first U.S. city where riders can access two fully driverless partners through the Uber app, he said. (Hyundai’s self-driving subsidiary Motional is also an Uber partner.)
That would give Uber riders a meaningful choice: a human driver or a robotaxi, and potentially even which autonomous service to use. And it could offer a revealing look at what customers actually prefer when given that choice. Price could tip the balance, too.
It makes me wonder whether Las Vegas will become the next battleground for organized labor as robotaxis begin competing directly with human drivers.
You might have seen the Wall Street Journal scoop that General Motors is working with an executive search firm to identify possible candidates to replace CEO Mary Barra . Rumors of her imminent departure have swirled for months, but this time there appears to be real work happening behind the scenes.
I reached out to a few little birds to learn more and here’s what they’re telling me. And, for the record, GM declined to comment.
GM has hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles, according to one source, who noted it’s possible that the board has other executive search firms working on this as well. The board is taking a two-track approach to its search, which is occurring simultaneously.
The first is focused on traditional yet transformative automotive CEOs. One name that has come up from the executive search firm is José Muñoz, who is president and CEO of Hyundai. The board is also interested in someone less traditional. The firm has apparently floated names like Doug Field, who recently became CEO of Mind Robotics, and Larry Culp of GE, according to a source with direct information.
There are internal GM folks who are also in the mix, including Sterling Anderson, co-founder of self-driving trucks company Aurora who became chief product officer at GM in May 2025, and Paul Jacobson, the company’s executive vice president and chief financial officer.

EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ and did not mention fossil fuels
The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey .
The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”
As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon in the longest climate summit ever, it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.
The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.
But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that some have said perpetuates fossil fuels.
The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.
But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.
“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”
Many countries, including the EU, UK and developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be main outcome of the Cop.
In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.
His intervention was met by applause from the hall, and was later followed by similar objections from Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway.
“This feels like a real line in the sand moment. Countries are standing up to fossil fuel interests and saying no,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics.
But Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, who called it “the worst Cop ever”, said: “The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create ... For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis.
“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves.”
Saudi Arabia defended the decision to include CCS in the text. Other countries, including the Africa group, China and Pakistan, also did not object to the deal, despite some having reservations. Pakistan told the conference that just because a few items in the pact were objectionable to some, the rest should not be sacrificed: “Climate action is not a menu from which we can select only what suits us.”
Ghana also had criticisms of the process but did not reject the final text: “Africa has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it.”
Close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya for a fortnight under the joint presidencies of Turkey and Australia, with the overrunning talks marked by long periods of deadlock as countries failed to find common ground.
The Cop co-president, Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, defended his leadership. “Australia left nothing on the field,” he said, but the red lines the presidencies had tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable”.
Asked about the consensus-based system that broke down at the talks, Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the UN framework convention on climate change, said: “It certainly fell short today,” while emphasising that a significant number of agenda items were passed, with “real progress and concrete results”.
But for many participants, these talks exposed a failure of collective will, particularly of the rich world, to confront the urgency of the climate crisis.
While extreme weather around the world has worsened this year, claiming tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves, in disasters such as the glacier collapse in Nepal, and in droughts and floods worsened by the supercharged El Niño , the slow speed of the climate negotiations appalled even veteran participants.
“There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues. That to me is very frustrating,” said Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and former UN climate envoy, as the talks neared their scheduled close. “We have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said: “I am deeply disappointed that Cop31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome. I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands. But this setback does not change the facts. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”

A powerful explosion aboard a Russian vessel docked at Libya’s eastern port of Benghazi has raised concerns that the Russia-Ukraine war could be extending into North Africa, after local authorities suggested the ship may have been targeted in a drone attack.
Officials from Libya’s eastern administration said the explosion occurred on Sunday while the Russian ship was stationed at the port for refuelling and resupply before returning to Russia.
No casualties were reported, although the incident prompted an emergency response and heightened security concerns around the port.
In an official statement, the eastern authorities indicated that drones were suspected of striking the vessel. No group or government immediately claimed responsibility.
The administration also emphasised that Libya was not involved in the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, seeking to distance the country from any suggestion that its territory was being used as a battleground in the ongoing war.
Early accounts of the explosion suggested that a fire had erupted at an ammunition storage facility within a naval installation in Benghazi. However, Libya’s eastern authorities subsequently clarified that the blast originated aboard a Russian ship docked at the port.
Local television reports described emergency crews being dispatched to the affected area to contain the fire and prevent it from spreading to nearby facilities.
Al-Masar television, citing civil defence personnel, reported that firefighters had been deployed to a military facility following the explosion. Libya Alhadath television also reported that residents were advised to avoid the surrounding area while emergency operations were underway. The fire was later brought under control.
Although Libyan authorities did not identify the vessel or disclose details of its cargo, naval analysts have provisionally identified it as the Russian missile corvette Merkury, which is believed to have sustained extensive damage in the explosion.
Libya’s eastern-based government announced plans to conduct a joint investigation with Russian officials to establish the circumstances surrounding the explosion.
The Benghazi incident comes against the backdrop of increasingly extensive Ukrainian operations targeting Russian military infrastructure, energy facilities and maritime assets beyond the conventional battlefield.
According to the supplied reports, a Russian cargo vessel was struck by a drone in the eastern Baltic Sea on Saturday , near Finnish waters. Finland’s military said Ukraine was likely responsible for the attack, although Kyiv has not claimed responsibility.
Although no evidence has been publicly presented linking Ukraine to the Benghazi explosion, the timing has drawn attention to the growing geographical reach of attacks associated with the war.
Russia has previously accused Ukraine of targeting vessels involved in transporting Russian energy exports, including ships operating far from the Black Sea.
The latest developments have raised questions about the vulnerability of commercial shipping routes, port facilities and maritime logistics networks in regions traditionally considered outside the immediate conflict zone.
The suspected strike has also exposed the security challenges facing Libya, where competing political authorities continue to exercise control over different parts of the country.
The internationally recognised Government of National Unity, based in Tripoli, expressed concern about the possibility of civilian maritime infrastructure being drawn into foreign military operations.
In a statement, the Tripoli administration warned against using Libyan ports and other civilian facilities for activities connected to international conflicts.
It stressed that Libya should not become a staging ground for foreign military confrontations or logistical operations that could threaten national security and sovereignty.
The statement reflects broader concerns that Libya’s strategic Mediterranean location, combined with its prolonged political fragmentation, could expose the country to escalating geopolitical tensions.
The Benghazi explosion follows other reported incidents involving Russian vessels in and around the Mediterranean.
In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier was severely damaged off the Libyan coast following an attack. Russian President Vladimir Putin blamed Ukraine for the incident, although responsibility remained a matter of dispute.
The vessel was reportedly associated with Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, a network of ships used to transport Russian energy exports while navigating Western sanctions and restrictions.
Ukraine has previously acknowledged operations against vessels linked to Russian maritime trade, including an attack in the Mediterranean in December of the previous year.
Such incidents have intensified concerns over the potential consequences of maritime attacks, particularly near civilian ports and international shipping corridors.
Apart from the immediate threat to vessels and crews, explosions involving ships can pose risks to port workers, coastal communities, commercial operations and the marine environment.
Russia has maintained longstanding military and political relationships with influential actors in eastern Libya, including forces associated with military commander Khalifa Haftar.
Libya’s geographical position makes it strategically important for access to the Mediterranean, North Africa and the wider Sahel region.
The country has remained politically divided since the 2011 uprising that overthrew longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi. The internationally recognised administration in Tripoli, headed by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, continues to face a rival eastern political and military establishment supported by Haftar.
This fragmentation has complicated efforts to establish unified national security institutions and limit foreign military involvement.
For now, significant questions remain unanswered, including whether the explosion was caused by a deliberate drone strike, who may have carried it out and whether the vessel was transporting military equipment.
The planned Libyan-Russian investigation may provide further information about the incident, although any conclusions will require examination of the available physical and technical evidence.
If a deliberate attack is confirmed, it would raise fresh concerns about the possibility of Russia’s war with Ukraine affecting ports and maritime facilities in North Africa.

No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia
A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.
The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government.
Initial reports said several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, triggering the explosion, the officials told the Associated Press.
Satellite imagery showed the Merkury had sunk after the attack, which took place in the Mediterranean, more than 1,000 miles from south Ukraine , marking a notable geographic expansion of the now near five-year war.
Though Ukraine began the war with no navy, it has developed a sea drone capability that threatened Russian warships in the Black Sea. The Russian fleet has been forced to retreat to the eastern port of Novorossiysk because Sevastopol in occupied Crimea had become unsafe.
Hours later, a Russia-linked cargo ship said to be carrying military supplies, the Ascalon, was hit by a sea drone off the coast of Benghazi. Video showed the drone heading directly towards one end of the vessel, again causing a huge explosion.
Libyan naval forces ‌rescued the vessel’s crew, the ‌sources added. The health ministry said some crew members were in stable condition with minor injuries. The number of injured and their nationalities are not known.
Benghazi is controlled by the self-styled Libyan National Army, led by Gen Khalifa Haftar, which controls eastern and southern Libya and has been aligned with Russia.
There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range attacks against Russia far beyond the frontlines.
The UN mission in Libya (Unsmil) expressed “serious concern” over the two drone attacks off Benghazi and called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”, in a post on X.
The ‌eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that ​normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.
It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and ⁠a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take ​legal and ​diplomatic measures against ​anyone found responsible.
“The Libyan government will not ​allow Libyan ‌ports, territory or territorial ​waters ​to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.
The specialist website Naval News earlier identified the ship attacked as the Merkury, a Russian corvette – the smallest class of warship, smaller than a frigate – and said it had almost certainly been destroyed.
HI Sutton, a naval analyst, said the attack was probably conducted by sea drones, after a photograph of one emerged apparently taken off the Libyan coast. The drone, he said, “is also likely the type used in the subsequent attack”. Similar-looking drones were involved in the subsequent attack on the Ascalon cargo ship.
If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the almost five-year war.
But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians on another continent and the working of the port.
A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.
Russian ships regularly make use of the port, which has a growing military importance to the Kremlin, to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean since the country lost its bases in Syria.
Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was ⁠struck by drones in the ⁠Baltic Sea continued to smoulder ​on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.
The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II ⁠on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly ⁠injured.
On Sunday, visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.
The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials. Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.
The risk of ⁠further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled ​out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public ​broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last ​week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.

The Democrats have won at least 258 seats in the 435-member House, gaining 44 from Republicans in its strongest general election performance since 1992.
The latest victory came in North Carolina, where Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated veteran Republican congresswoman Virginia Foxx. Four House races have yet to be decided, with contests in Minnesota and Tennessee still awaiting a result and two Louisiana races heading to runoffs in December.
The result surpasses the Democrats' gains in the 2018 midterm elections, when they picked up 40 seats during Trump's first presidency. Republicans are now set to hold no more than 177 seats, leaving them with one of their smallest House delegations in decades.
The Democratic wave extended across traditional Republican strongholds, the Midwest and the East Coast, reflecting widespread voter frustration over the cost of living, the war in Iran and allegations of corruption surrounding the Trump administration.
Democrats will also control the Senate, where they have secured 56 seats, giving the party its strongest position in Congress in more than a decade.
With control of both chambers from January, Democrats are preparing an ambitious first 100 days focused on household finances, healthcare and government accountability.
Their priorities include reversing Republican cuts to Medicaid and restoring Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired under Republican control. The party also intends to use congressional investigative powers to scrutinise Trump's administration, including the financial interests of the president and his family.
Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader, is expected to become the first Black Speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes on 3 January 2027.
Unlike outgoing Republican Speaker Mike Johnson, who struggled to manage a razor-thin majority, Jeffries would have considerable room to accommodate disagreements between progressive and moderate Democrats.
Nevertheless, the scale of the victory has raised expectations that the party will produce tangible results.
“Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure,” Democratic congressman Jason Crow of Colorado told the Associated Press, pointing to Americans struggling with healthcare costs, economic insecurity and immigration enforcement.
Progressive congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez described the election result as “a mandate for change”, while centrist Democrat Tom Suozzi argued that the party should devote most of its attention to affordability rather than investigations.
The Democratic takeover threatens to significantly constrain Trump during the final two years of his presidency.
Congressional committees are expected to launch investigations into the administration, potentially issuing subpoenas and demanding testimony from senior officials. Jeffries has also declined to rule out a third impeachment attempt against Trump.
The White House has responded aggressively, suggesting that some proposed investigations could amount to criminal misconduct — a claim that has intensified tensions over Congress's constitutional oversight responsibilities.
Republicans, meanwhile, face a difficult period of rebuilding. Jim Jordan of Ohio, chosen to lead the party's diminished House minority, has pledged to fight for American families and regain political ground ahead of the 2028 elections.
For Democrats, however, the immediate challenge is turning an overwhelming electoral victory into effective government. Their substantial congressional majorities offer an unusual opportunity to advance legislation, but Trump's continued control of the White House means major bills could still face a presidential veto.
Fact is: The midterm elections have fundamentally shifted the balance of power in Washington.

Democrat Chuck Hubbard was elected to the US House of Representatives from North Carolina on Sunday after defeating veteran Republican Virginia Foxx, who chairs the powerful House Rules Committee. His victory gave Democrats their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in the 2026 US midterms.
House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.
Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Donald Trump ’s first midterm in 2018.
The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.
The milestone in the 435-member House sets up divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House . Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address high costs of living while also confronting Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term in office.
The Democrats’ majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt-era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.
“Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure,” said Democratic Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, a former Army Ranger.
“There are people dying in this country and people losing their healthcare, losing their livelihoods, losing their farms, being terrorized from ICE," he said earlier this month at the Capitol, referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. "If you don't feel a sense of urgency and pressure in this job, and a desperation to deliver for folks, then you don't belong under this Capitol dome."
The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and the Iran war and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Trump.
Read more Peltola defeats Sullivan in Alaska Senate race, expanding Democratic majority
Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.
The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans’ Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.
Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.
“This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen,” said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez , D-N.Y., at the Capitol.
Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability.
“Everything should be tied back to the people — and how it’s affecting the people,” he said.
For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: “How does that affect people’s pocketbooks?”
The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to “blatant criminality.”
After House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow single-digit majority — meaning a few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda — the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver.
Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition.
"We're not a monolith — people come to the caucus with different ideas — it's OK,” said Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.
Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.
Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio , who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.
“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families,” Jordan said.
The GOP's high-water marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

At least 258 US House seats are now under Democratic control, with four more midterm races yet to be decided.
The Democratic Party has won at least 258 seats in the United States House of Representatives, its highest total since 1992.
On Sunday, a congressional race in North Carolina was decided after a recount, giving Democrats their 258th House seat, as a handful of races in the 2026 midterm elections are still being counted.
The race for North Carolina’s 5th congressional district saw Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeat Republican incumbent Virginia Foxx, who has served 11 terms in Congress.
The win was symbolic of a larger political shift in North Carolina and elsewhere, as longtime Republican strongholds flipped to Democratic hands, sometimes for the first time in decades.
Foxx was first elected in 2004, and in recent years, she was the chair of the House Rules Committee. According to The Associated Press news agency, only 330 votes separated Hubbard and Foxx as of Sunday, when the race was called in the Democrat’s favour.
Four House races have yet to be called, meaning Democrats may still expand their already sizeable majority in the 435-member House.
The party has now picked up about 47 House seats. Currently, in the outgoing Congress, Democrats hold 214 seats.
But the House was not the only congressional chamber to flip in this year’s midterm elections.
In the 120th Congress, set to be sworn in on January 3, Democrats will also hold 56 seats in the US Senate, its largest majority in more than a decade.
Those majorities give the Democratic Party significant power over legislation, although President Donald Trump, a Republican, has already pledged to veto bills the party puts forward.
Experts say the Republican Party’s drubbing in the midterm elections was driven by voter frustration with issues like the cost of living, the US-Israel war on Iran, corruption and immigration raids.
It was also widely interpreted as a referendum on Trump’s second term, which began in 2025.
As of November, only 32 percent of Americans approved of Trump’s job performance, according to a poll by the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos.
Democrats have framed their electoral victory as a unique opportunity to shape the final two years of Trump’s presidency.
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a progressive who won her re-election bid in New York’s 14th congressional district, called the political shift a “mandate for change”.
“This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen,” Ocasio-Cortez said at the US Capitol.
The party’s majority in the House will be larger than any since Democrat Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 with a 258-seat majority for his party.
It is also just above the 257 seats held by Democrats when Barack Obama was elected in 2008.

Exclusive: Statement on death of Australian music industry legend drafted using search and AI but ‘fact checked and edited’ before approval, party says
Tributes flow for Molly Meldrum: Human Nature, Jason Donovan and others remember music industry great
A statement on the death of Molly Meldrum attributed to the Victorian opposition leader, Jess Wilson , was written using AI, the Liberal party has confirmed.
Meldrum, the Australian music journalist, broadcaster and producer, died on Monday morning . He was 83. Shortly after his death, Wilson issued a statement describing Meldrum as a “true Australian icon who will never be forgotten”.
“His famous cowboy hat, his larger-than-life personality and his lifelong love for his beloved Saints made him unmistakably Molly,” the statement read.
“But above all, he will be remembered for his generosity, his warmth and the enormous affection Australians held for him.”
When submitted to AI-detector service Pangram, the 177-word statement came up as 100% AI-authored. Pangram maintains its algorithm is so accurate that it incorrectly identifies text as an AI output only about one in every 10,000 times.
In response to questions from Guardian Australia, a Liberal party spokesperson confirmed the party used AI to compile research on Meldrum’s career and draft the statement.
“Like plenty of workplaces, we use search and AI to help with drafting and researching a variety of material, which was the case here,” the spokesperson said.
“The initial draft was done using a combination of search and AI to compile Molly’s extensive career.”
It is understood the initial AI-generated draft did not include references to Meldrum’s time on TV variety show, Hey Hey It’s Saturday or the two times he was crowned as the king of Melbourne’s Moomba festival. That information was added by a member of the team.
“The statement was then fact checked and edited by a member of the team before it was provided to the Leader for approval,” the spokesperson said. “The final version pays tribute to a true legend of the Australian entertainment industry.”
A tribute by the premier, Ben Carroll, came up as 100% human-authored when submitted to Pangram.
In it, the Victorian Labor leader described the Sunday night tradition of tuning into Meldrum’s Countdown program and then heading to a record shop on Monday morning to ask for the song he recommended.
This article includes content provided by Instagram . We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue' .
“Molly gave young Australian musicians a chance to be heard in lounge rooms across the country,” Carroll’s statement said.
“Years before Countdown, he helped start the St Kilda cheer squad. Supporting others was in his nature. A giant of the Australian music industry and a true character.”
Carroll said Meldrum would be honoured with a state funeral.
AI has been used extensively during the Victorian election campaign by the major parties and One Nation, as well as third-party campaigners. Labor’s release of a deepfake video of Wilson trick-or-treating alongside One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, was widely criticised and prompted the Greens to call for the practice to be banned altogether.
Timothy Koskie, a media researcher at the University of Sydney, said authenticity is becoming a “harder currency to build” due to the prevalence of AI.
“The public is doubting the credibility, authenticity, reliability of just about everything in the shared social space,” he said.
Last month, the Australian Electoral Commissioner, Jeff Pope, told the federal parliamentary inquiry on artificial intelligence that there would be challenges in requiring political communications to be labelled if AI was used in its creation.
“The challenge with that is that, if AI is not already ubiquitous, it’s not far away,” he said. “If you’re labelling everything with AI, then, at the next election or not too long thereafter, every bit of political communication could have an AI label on it, and you’ve got to wonder about the effectiveness of that.”
