COP31 President Murat Kurum, center, leaves a closing plenary session at the U.N. Climate Summit, Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from fossil fuels like coal and natural gas. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption
ANTALYA, Turkey – International climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours with a disagreement over how to address fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
On Sunday, delegates from nearly 200 countries failed to reach an overall agreement covering targets for electrification, finance to help developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change, and how to respond to the fact that the planet will soon breach a key warming threshold.
The talks ran two days longer than expected, becoming the longest climate conference in the history of these summits. And it ended in a dramatic fashion, with delegates from the European Union rejecting any final outcome that did not explicitly call for a transition away from fossil fuels. Some oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed such language. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal makes up roughly 73% of global emissions .
Ireland's Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O'Brien, who spoke for the EU, soon left the room, along with EU Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth Wopke Hoekstra.
Other countries also objected to the text, including Panama, Belize, and small island states such as Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands.
Hoekstra said that with the world heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."
This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been formal acknowledgment that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to try to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.
Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts , like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035 . That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.
Meanwhile, the transition away from fossil fuels is happening regardless of what the U.N. agreements say, says Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who ran the negotiations.
Negotiations at this year's U.N. Climate Summit were supposed to end Friday but there was no agreement on language about fossil fuels. Activists demonstrated by holding signs that read "shame" at COP31, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption
"The transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is inevitable," Bowen told the press after the agreement failed. "It's happening at speed and it's irreversible."
The disagreements over mentioning fossil fuels in climate conferences have a long, fractured history.
The COP process works by consensus, so nearly 200 countries must agree to a final text at the end of the negotiations. Some fossil fuel producers like Norway and Mexico have recently wanted to include transitioning away from fossil fuels in the text. Other large oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia and Russia have blocked adding fossil fuels to the final agreement.
At the climate talks in Dubai in 2023, countries agreed for the first time in 28 years of conferences to mention transitioning away from fossil fuels in the final agreement.
Deeply frustrated with this U.N. process, more than 50 countries have created their own separate conference dedicated to phasing out fossil fuels. In April, they held the "First International Conference for the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels" in Colombia. In 2027, Ireland and the Pacific Island nation of Tuvalu will co-host the second conference.
These side efforts are the best hope for climate action until something changes in the COP process, says Juan Carlos Navarro, environment minister of Panama.
"I am an optimist by nature," he tells NPR, "but I am not an idiot."
This year, the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and the unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz loomed over the negotiations.
Since the war began, countries across Asia and Africa have accelerated their transitions to solar energy, batteries and electric vehicles, and reduced their reliance on fossil fuels like oil and natural gas .
COP31 organizers promised that this would be the "electrification COP." Climate technologies like renewable energy, super-efficient heat pumps and electric vehicles are also called electrification technologies. Many of these technologies are being manufactured in China, the main exporter of climate solutions.
The conference's initial goal was to increase global electrification from its current level of around 23% to 35% by 2035. "So 35 by '35 is the mantra," Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember, told NPR when COP31 began.
The 35 by 35 electrification pledge was signed on to by dozens of countries. However, that pledge did not ultimately pass, says Alden Meyer, a senior associate at the climate change think tank E3G. "Electrification was collateral damage when the whole decision cratered," he said.
The Trump administration did not send a delegation to COP31 for a second year in a row. President Trump announced he would withdraw the U.S. from the Paris Agreement on his first day back in office in 2025. Trump has called climate change a hoax, and his administration has rolled back regulations on climate pollution and funding for wind and solar power and electric vehicles.
An informal delegation of congressional Democrats did come to Turkey. They told delegates at COP31 that when Democrats control both chambers of Congress next year, climate change will return to the main agenda.
While the debate over fossil fuels stole the spotlight at this year's COP, a major focus of the negotiations has been on money. Countries debated new goals for funding to assist nations hardest hit by climate change.
Over the years at climate summits, lower-income countries have made the case that while they're responsible for only a small share of the emissions causing climate change, they're experiencing some of the worst disasters.
"We're not a nation that has the luxury of debating whether climate change is real for us," says Matthew Samuda, Jamaica's minister of water, environment and climate change. "The reality is, over the last five years, we have had a category 4 hurricane, a tropical storm and a category 5 hurricane. So climate change for us is indeed real and we are experiencing economic losses from a problem that we didn't create."
In 2024, nations agreed to eventually provide $1.3 trillion per year to developing nations, what's known as climate finance. Only about $136.7 billion was delivered in 2024 , according to a report from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. The majority of that goes to projects that reduce emissions, including renewable energy like solar and wind.
As climate disasters become costlier, lower-income countries have been pushing for more funding to adapt to climate impacts, such as protecting coastal communities from sea level rise and strengthening infrastructure against storms. The United Nations estimates that those nations' needs will reach $305 billion annually by 2035 .
The COP31 U.N. Climate Summit ended Sunday in Antalya, Turkey and tens of thousands of people attended what has become the longest summit in the history of these gatherings. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption
During the talks in Turkey, developing nations pushed for more concrete commitments to deliver adaptation funding…

Green shoots of recovery have lasted longer in a blast furnace than in the Mauricio Pochettino era at Manchester United . On another abysmal Anfield day for the fallen giants of Manchester, Pochettino endured a baptism of fire from the eighth minute onwards when Leny Yoro was sent off for denying Alexander Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity. Liverpool would not be denied anything else while tormenting their old rivals yet again.
Andoni Iraola indulged in his first fist-pumps towards the Kop after an utterly dominant, comfortable win illuminated by Rio Ngumoha and Florian Wirtz brilliance plus goals from Dominik Szoboszlai and Víctor Muñoz. Liverpool’s two creative forces were also on the scoresheet as Ngumoha became the youngster scorer in the fixture’s Premier League history.
“Poch is at the wheel” was the mocking, merciless soundtrack that accompanied the end of the former Tottenham, Chelsea and USA coach’s first traumatic game in the job. There may well be more. On this evidence, 19th in the Premier League is not a misleading reflection of United’s position.
The latest calamity in United’s worst start to a season for 40 years cannot be pinned on a head coach who met his new charges only on Wednesday. There can be no genuine takes on Pochettino’s vision for United either, given how quickly he was forced to turn his first game into a damage-limitation exercise. But there was one firm conclusion to be drawn. His first big call in the job proved a serious mistake with destructive repercussions for United’s entire evening.
That ill-fated decision was to hand Matthijs de Ligt a first Premier League start in 12 months at the expense of Harry Maguire. Maguire may be a symbol of United’s inertia, but his replacement at centre-back was heavily responsible for the chaos that quickly unfolded. The Netherlands international was at fault for three goals. Liverpool , under instruction from Iraola to start strong and “make them feel pressure from the beginning”, could hardly believe their luck at the first mishap in the visitors’ central defence.
• Accounting for 3pts/win all-time, Manchester United’s eight points this season are their fewest after 11 games of a league campaign since 1972-73 (7). That is also the previous season in which the Red Devils managed only one win through their first 11 league matches.
• Mauricio Pochettino (pictured) suffered the joint-heaviest defeat by a Manchester United manager in his first game (0-4), along with a defeat by the same scoreline for Lal Hilditch in October 1926 (0-4 v Bolton Wanderers in the top flight).
• Manchester United end the day in 19th position in the Premier League, with this the first time since November 1986 that they have been within the bottom two places of the league table having played at least 10 matches (21st in that case).
• Mauricio Pochettino was the first manager in Premier League history to see his team concede twice and receive a red card in the first half of his first match in charge of a club. Opta
De Ligt lost the flight of the ball and his man, Isak, when Ronald Araújo pinged a routine pass down Liverpool’s right-hand channel. Isak was suddenly away, De Ligt all at sea, and to compound matters Yoro was slow to react to the danger. By the time United’s covering defender was across to challenge Isak it was too late. Yoro clattered into the back of the Sweden international just outside the area and was shown a straight red card by the referee, Sam Barrott. Isak’s heavy first touch could not save Yoro. The free-kick could not save United from double jeopardy. Szoboszlai swept a powerful set piece into Senne Lammens’ bottom right-hand corner from 19 yards.
Pochettino claimed the dismissal was wrong and United should have had a penalty moments earlier for a Jérémy Jacquet challenge on Bryan Mbeumo. It was a desperate take. A simple detail showed the extent of the job United’s latest head coach has on his hands: the wall that lined up to face Szoboszlai’s free-kick. Just getting that right was beyond this group of players. White shirts lined up to protect the left side of Lammens’ goal but, with the isolated exception of Bruno Fernandes, no one covered the spot where the ball was ultimately placed.
Liverpool devoured the gifts. When the hosts doubled their lead three minutes later thoughts of another 7-0 humiliation for United did not seem unreasonable. Ngumoha tormented Diogo Dalot from the first whistle, as everyone inside the ground expected he would. Having been found by Isak’s cross-field pass the teenager breezed past Dalot to the byline and lifted a cross slightly behind Wirtz. The German playmaker, left in space by De Ligt, improvised brilliantly to hook a volley into the roof of the net while floating in mid-air. United were sinking into the abyss.
The first chants of “sacked in the morning” flowed from the Kop towards a disbelieving United head coach. There were 14 minutes on the clock. It was, of course, a ludicrous chant. It might be months before United’s hapless owners are seeking another scapegoat.
Pochettino responded in the only way he could to the onslaught and introduced Maguire into a rejigged five-man defence. Whether in the knowledge that United possessed neither the ability nor the inclination to hurt them, Liverpool eased off for the remainder of the first half although Isak and Alexis Mac Allister could have extended the lead.
• Since the start of the 2021-22 season, Liverpool's four wins by 4+ goals against Manchester United are the most any Premier League team has achieved against another across all competitions.
• Andoni Iraola is unbeaten in his seven Premier League matches against Manchester United (W3 D4). The only manager to record a longer unbeaten run against the Red Devils in the competition is Jürgen Klopp (8 between 2018 and 2022).
• This was the quickest Liverpool had gone 2-0 up in a Premier League match against Manchester United, going two ahead after just 12 minutes and 40 seconds.
• Rio Ngumoha (18y 85d) became the youngest player to score and assist in a Premier League game for Liverpool since Michael Owen on Boxing Day 1997 (18y 12d v Leeds United).
• Dominik Szoboszlai (pictured) scored his fifth direct free kick for Liverpool in the Premier League; only Jamie Redknapp (8), Steven Gerrard (7) and Trent Alexander-Arnold (6) have netted more for the club in the competition.
• Florian Wirtz created 10 chances in open play for Liverpool, the most by a player in a Premier League match since Manchester City’s David Silva against West Brom in March 2015 (11). Opta
Liverpool did not let their rivals off so lightly after the restart. Bradley Barcola could and should have provided Wirtz with a hat-trick of assists but squandered three beautiful touches from his fellow £100m+ recruit. Virgil van Dijk put a free header wide from another fine delivery by Wirtz. Barcola turned provider in devastating style, however, to create the goal Ngumoha’s display richly deserved. The France winger burst away from Lisandro Martínez and Fernandes with one flick of the ball before delivering an assist on a plate for the teenager to convert.
Iraola’s thoughts started to drift towards the midweek Champions League trip to Club Brugge and he started resting players from the 72nd minute onwards. But Liverpool were not done. Another mistake by De Ligt, this time a sloppy pass infield, was pounced on by Wirtz who released Muñoz inside the box. The Liverpool substitute stroked an emphatic finish past Lammens. All Sir Alex Ferguson could do up in the directors’ box in the closing stages was laugh with his friend the actor James Nesbit. The alternative is too bleak for a proud United man to contemplate.

Dozens of militant Israeli settlers raided communities on Saturday night, setting fire to vehicles and several homes
Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.
Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.
Photographs from Kafr Malik , near Ramallah, showed one slogan written in Hebrew that read: “This is the first revenge.” Several vehicles and homes had been set alight in the village.
Images from nearby Deir al-Sudan showed vehicles on fire. Palestinian reports said an agricultural building had been set ablaze in Deir Ballut and cars torched in Deir Abu Mashal.
An ⁠inconclusive election last month stripped Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, of his majority. Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.
“Last night’s arson attacks in Judea and Samaria were acts of Jewish terrorism, in every sense of the term,” Eisenkot said, using the biblical name for the West Bank. “Extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations.”
Referring to the far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, he added: “The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy.”
Eisenkot, who has been given 28 days to form a government by the president, Isaac Herzog, with a possible 14-day extension, urged the government and security establishment to “use every tool at their disposal – including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet – to stop the rioters and impose harsh sanctions on them”.
In an unprecedented rebuke on Sunday, several other members of the Israeli parliament criticised Netanyahu over escalating violence by militant settlers against Palestinians.
Yair Lapid, the leader of Yesh Atid, held Netanyahu’s government responsible for encouraging the attacks. “Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence by the Israeli government,” he said on X, adding that ministers were deliberately encouraging the militant settlers’ violence “through their silence”.
Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, warned of the possibility of a third intifada and described the West Bank as “on the brink of an explosion”.
“Anyone who wants to prevent a third intifada must replace the current government, which provides cover and support for Jewish terrorism and abandons security,” Golan said on X. “Jewish terrorism harms innocent Palestinians and Israeli army soldiers, and pushes Israel toward unprecedented international isolation.”
Noam Tibon, a retired army major general and Knesset member, gave a similar warning. “If Israel does not eliminate Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, it will destroy Israel,” he wrote.
Australia announced sanctions on Wednesday against three people and four Israeli entities, including a construction company, over their role in the expansion of illegal settlements and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
A day earlier the UK imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, which the UN regards as Palestinian territory under Israeli occupation since 1967.
Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.
On Tuesday, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli militant settlers in a village near Jericho, where the group has recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.

Watch: Democrat who unseated 21-year Republican incumbent says party needs to 'bring change'
The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.
The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.
The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.
Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.
Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.
"I think the American people are just sick of what's going on and they wanted a change. They voted for change," Hubbard told the BBC News Channel after his victory. He pledged to work alongside his fellow lawmakers to hold President Donald Trump accountable.
Earlier, he wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".
Hubbard added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."
Foxx, meanwhile, said in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."
Virginia Foxx spent a decade in the North Carolina Senate before representing the state in the House of Representatives
Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.
Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.
Trump himself - as well as Vice President JD Vance - have suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses.
Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.
The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.

A suspected Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship Sunday at a naval base in Libya , officials said, the latest attack in the North African nation linked to the Russia-Ukraine war.
The strike at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, and ignited a fire at the facility, two Libyan military officials told the Associated Press.
They said that several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, they said.
The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.
Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime dictator Muammar Gaddafi , who was later killed, in 2011. A UN-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is located in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.

The eastern Libya-based government said in a statement that the strike on Sunday caused an explosion and fire at the base, which was later extinguished.
The vessel had docked at the base for refueling and supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said, without providing details on the vessel or its cargo.
A joint investigation was launched with Russia to “uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it,” the statement said.
No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack. There was no immediate comment from either Russia or Ukraine .

Jay Clayton was pressed on Trump’s characterization of Putin during media appearances on Sunday
Jay Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, said he trusts Donald Trump “completely” after the US president called Vladimir Putin “a friend” during their recent meeting in China.
Clayton made the remarks on Sunday, where he was pressed during media appearances on Trump’s warm characterization of the Russian president – who is viewed as a chief US adversary – following his trilateral summit with Putin and China’s Xi Jinping. After a backlash at home and aboard, Trump doubled down on Saturday and posted a photo of himself and Putin shaking hands with the caption “My Friend.”
On CNN’s State of the Union, Dana Bash asked Clayton whether he also thinks Putin is a friend to the US.
“The president is the greatest conductor of foreign policy in a very challenging time that we have seen,” said Clayton on Sunday. “Getting the three nuclear powers together and getting them to agree that they are not going to escalate, that they are going to communicate, that is historic. That is remarkable and, in that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely.”
Bash pressed on whether Clayton personally agrees that Putin should be considered a friend.
“Dana, in different contexts, you can use different words. The president pulling off that summit, getting the three of them together, is just remarkable,” Clayton replied.
Speaking with ABC’s Jonathan Karl on This Week, Clayton made similar comments, saying that “using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate” in the context of the summit.
“That conversation, that picture – historic, historic picture – was in the context of the three nuclear powers, the three main nuclear powers, getting together and saying, ‘We cannot have a nuclear incident,’” Clayton said on Sunday, referring to Trump’s post. “In that circle of that conversation, using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate.”
Clayton also dodged when asked again whether he thinks Putin should be considered a friend to the United States.
“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton responded.
Last week, Trump sidestepped questions about his views on a friendship with Putin.
“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said in a press briefing. “I have fantastic relationships with Putin, that’s a very good thing.”
Trump’s characterization of Putin has sparked backlash from US lawmakers and officials abroad.
“Who is he? He’s the man who has abducted tens of thousands of children, killed tens of thousands of civilians, targeted civilian infrastructure across Ukraine, detained Americans wrongfully, and continues to do so daily,” Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer posted on social media.
“Embarrassing, despicable, and quite frankly pathetic,” Schumer added. “Senate Democrats will always stand with Ukraine and against Putin and autocratic dictators around the world.”
“It’s beyond me,” Senator Jeanne Shaheen said in an interview with MS NOW. “I don’t understand the president’s admiration and cozying up to Vladimir Putin, who is a war criminal.”
Trump’s comments also drew rebukes abroad, including from the deputy leader of the rightwing party Reform UK.
“It’s just wrong at every level … And it’s a grave mistake,” Richard Tice told Sky News. “He is not our friend, Putin. He is, as others have said, a murderous dictator. And no one is in any doubt about that.”
Trump’s description of ​Putin as a friend also drew criticism from European ​allies of Ukraine. “Mr ‌Putin is ​not our ​friend and will never be,” the Polish prime minister Donald Tusk said.
Separately, Clayton also faced questions about the recent spate of technology outages across the US and said Americans should expect more disruptions as companies and government agencies replace aging systems.
“And ​as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, ⁠interruptions in service,” Clayton said on CNN’s State of the Union program. “That is ⁠going to happen.”

Report and free match highlights as Manchester United are routed by Liverpool at Anfield in Mauricio Pochettino's first game; Leny Yoro received early red card before Liverpool ran riot; defeat keeps Man Utd in relegation zone, one point off bottom
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
Mauricio Pochettino endured a horror start to his Manchester United tenure as his 10-man side were thrashed 4-0 by Liverpool at Anfield following Leny Yoro's early sending off.
Yoro saw red in the eighth minute when he was adjudged to have made a last-man foul on Alexander Isak, with Dominik Szoboszlai slamming home the resulting free-kick.
The decision was contentious, with Isak having seemingly lost control of the ball when he was fouled, but the double blow left the visitors in disarray and Florian Wirtz added an acrobatic second only two minutes and 46 seconds after the opener.
Liverpool fans taunted Pochettino with chants of 'you're getting sacked in the morning' following the second goal.
The Argentine's decision to hand Matthijs de Ligt a first Premier League start in 357 days backfired spectacularly, with the 27-year-old misjudging a high ball in the lead-up to Yoro's red card before the hosts punished more shambolic defending after the break.
Rio Ngumoha added the third when he converted Bradley Barcola's low cross following a rapid counter-attack, becoming the youngest scorer in the history of the fixture, with substitute Victor Munoz netting the fourth from a through ball by the excellent Wirtz.
The four-goal loss showed Pochettino the size of the task ahead and keeps United in the Premier League relegation zone, only a point off the bottom. They have conceded more goals than any other side in Europe's major leagues in all competitions, with 34.
The scoreline could easily have been worse for them, with Barcola and Isak among those to miss chances as Liverpool racked up 28 shots, 10 of which came from Wirtz passes.
The defeat was the heaviest in a Manchester United manager's first game since Lal Hilditch was beaten by the same scoreline a century ago, in 1926. It is the first time in 40 years that United have been in the bottom two at this stage of a season.
For Pochettino's counterpart Andoni Iraola, the result represents his first statement win since taking charge. Liverpool move back into fourth place, only a point behind Manchester City in third and seven points behind leaders Arsenal.
Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino to Sky Sports :
"So painful. So disappointed. It's not okay to start a game in the Premier League with this situation.
"The game changed completely after six minutes. Now we can explain everything but the damage is done, it's so painful.
"The players are so, so feeling the pain of the result. I told them to be calm: it was an unfair situation that happened.
"We need to accept that reality. We need to try to increase our focus, concentration and make better decisions on the field.
"We also need to be critical on ourselves but some situations happened in the game that we are not happy."
"I enjoyed it. I have to do a lot more but I think we wanted to celebrate in that moment. It's nice to enjoy it with the fans.
"The supporters deserved it. We've been very good away and not good enough at home. It's always a big game against Man Utd.
"They played with 10 for most of the game but we still did our job.
"We created enough to score more than four, we missed chances.
"We need to be more ruthless, but luckily today it was not needed."
Sky Sports pundit Gary Neville : "This is where we've got to, where we're starting to write off 4-0 defeats at Anfield as if it's just the norm and what should be accepted.
"But the fan standards haven't dropped. They expect a Manchester United team to be competitive every single week, and what they're seeing now - Manchester United have got the worst defence in the whole of Europe, and they're currently second from bottom in the Premier League.
Sky Sports pundit Roy Keane : "United were desperate. So bad.
"Gary Neville's okay with 4-0? Are you telling me they could have done better? Four-nil is not too bad with 10 men? Has anyone ever got a result with 10 men? It can be done!
"People who played for the club said 4-0 is not too bad? Wow. Fans are applauding. Applauding what?
"We're blaming the board, blaming ownership, blaming managers. When do the players take responsibility for some decision-making?
"Liverpool probably should have scored eight, probably eight or nine. It's unbelievable chances they had.
"And everyone's coming off the pitch saying four is not too bad? I feel like swearing."

Army invokes emergency provisions in Iowa to avoid court order despite worries about health and environment risks
The US army plans to invoke emergency provisions to avoid a court order that had put on hold plans to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa , saying that continued delays will make it more dangerous as the weather starts to turn colder.
“To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action,” government lawyers told the eight US circuit court of appeals in a filing late on Saturday. “Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay.”
Environmental groups criticized the government’s move, decrying it as a maneuver to get around a court order and avoid public demands for safety and transparency.
The appeals court on Thursday granted a request by environmentalists to put on hold a permit that cleared the way for the detonation in Middletown, a small community about 160 miles (257km) south-east of Des Moines. It was initially planned for Friday, but the army later announced that it would push the operation to Monday after an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.
Environmentalists have called for a review of the emergency permit that was approved earlier this month by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
In a statement on Sunday, the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club and Earthjustice questioned claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration.
“The Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public’s demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm,” said Thien Chau, an attorney at Earthjustice.
Government lawyers said the army doesn’t need a permit to take emergency action against an immediate threat from explosive material.
They said the standards of a federal law regulating hazardous waste don’t apply in situations when there is an immediate threat to health, safety or the environment as determined by an explosive or munitions emergency response specialist.
Officials contend that the chemicals are unstable, and the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop. They said there is a risk that the chemicals may explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30F (-1C) in the coming days.
In March, staff at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant found several dozen barrels of degraded lead azide, which is used in munitions production. Crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan.
According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums’ contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.
The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their petition that other alternatives were not fully considered. They also criticized officials for not sharing more information with the public.
Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground.
Iowans in the region were told to stay inside, keep windows and doors closed, bring pets and livestock indoors, and clean cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces after.
“The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” an advisory states. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals.”

"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."
The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.
The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.
In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days.
"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.
It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".
The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.
Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.
On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible.
Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.
The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".
One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen.

The US Army plans to invoke emergency powers to detonate 4 tonnes of lead azide in an Iowa town, despite a court-ordered stay.
The United States Army intends to detonate more than 4 tonnes of lead azide at a military base in Iowa, defying a federal appeals court’s order suspending its permit to do so.
In a fact sheet this weekend, the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services said that two controlled explosions were scheduled for around noon (06:00 GMT) on Monday.
That announcement follows statements from the Department of Justice, arguing that Tuesday was the cut-off date to carry out a planned detonation.
Lead azide is a key explosive used in military ammunition. The Iowa stockpile has reportedly grown unstable, and Justice Department lawyers have warned that sub-freezing temperatures could trigger an uncontrolled explosion.
“The real choice, in other words, is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is between a planned and mitigated detonation and an unplanned and unmitigated explosion,” their court filing said.
But critics have questioned the army’s rationale for pushing ahead with the planned detonation, despite the court order to pause it.
“Anyone can claim an emergency at any point and do whatever they want. I don’t think people can or should accept that,” said Thien Chau, a lawyer with the legal group Earthjustice, which represents the plaintiffs in the lawsuit.
Chau told Al Jazeera that not enough has been done to mitigate the risk from the explosions, which are expected to release a cloud of lead into the air.
Experts say there is no safe level of lead exposure, and the dense metal can cause birth defects, brain damage and infertility.
“Anyone who hears that the army plans to explode nearly 10,000 pounds [4,500kg] of [this chemical] would recognise that that is not normal,” Chau said.
“That is extraordinary, and that is not something that you just take lightly.”
The impending explosions come after a tense legal battle between the US government and environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council.
The groups have questioned the legality of an emergency permit the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) granted on November 13. The EPA authorised the Army to move forward with the explosions, originally scheduled for November 20.
The plaintiffs pointed out that nearby residents were only given a week’s notice and that the blasts could send lead dust as far as 160km (100 miles).
They also argued that the EPA failed to properly assess safer disposal methods.
The US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit granted a pause on Friday. But in a Saturday court filing, the Justice Department maintained that the Army could still proceed with the two controlled blasts under an emergency exemption.
“The emergency exception does not depend on the Emergency Permit and is therefore not affected by, nor contradictory to, the terms of this Court’s administrative stay,” the Justice Department said in its filing.
But Earthjustice has argued that such a manoeuvre would sidestep the court’s authority.
Government lawyers have “laid the groundwork for a possible detonation without a permit, which would effectively bypass judicial process and review”, lawyer Rachel Rintelmann wrote in a Friday filing.
The controversy centres on a deteriorating stockpile of explosives stored for more than two decades at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near the city of Middletown.
The stockpile contains roughly 9,700 pounds (4.4 tonnes) of lead azide across 68 barrels, with lead accounting for approximately 6,900 pounds (about 3.1 tonnes) of its chemical mass.
The explosives had been kept in a mixture of water and ethanol to ensure their stability. But in March, military technicians at the facility discovered that the system was breaking down.
According to a court declaration , an Army munitions expert found that the liquid in the drums had evaporated, causing needle-shaped crystals to form.
That recrystallisation puts the lead azide at risk of exploding on its own, as a result of temperature charges or even friction. So many crystals had formed that it was no longer safe to even open the barrels, according to the expert.
But on Sunday, Earthjustice released a statement questioning how this problem was allowed to develop in the first place.
“This emergency is of the Army’s own making,” the statement said. “The Army has not publicly provided details about why the lead azide was not disposed of before it became so dangerous. ”
The US Army has said the barrels are set to be detonated in place at the Iowa facility.
But it claims to have explored other options as well. According to the Army’s environmental assessment , it has previously considered two alternatives: chemically neutralising the explosives, or transporting them to an on-site detonation facility.
It rejected both ideas due to concerns that handling or transporting the explosives could trigger an accidental detonation.
Burying the drums, meanwhile, risked subjecting the shock-sensitive material to jolts that could similarly cause an unintended explosion.
But the health risks of even a planned explosion have put residents and environmental groups on edge.
On November 15, the Army released two plume maps outlining the potential spread of lead contamination across a swath of eastern Iowa, though projections hinge on real-time wind conditions.
The first map traces what could happen if a lead-bearing plume drifts northward, with a potential airborne trajectory over communities like Burlington, Muscatine, Davenport, Iowa City and Cedar Rapids.
The second map presents a more tenacious problem: surface exposure.
As the plume tracks north, heavier lead-bearing particles are expected to coat the landscape, landing on outdoor furniture, cars, soil and crops.
Residents in the projected plume path were advised to shelter indoors with their pets, shut windows, and limit exposure to outdoor air during a precautionary period, pending the Army’s all-clear.
Those living near Middletown City Park and Butterfly Park were also instructed to leave their homes for six hours to avoid ground vibrations that could crack or shatter nearby windows.
In the plume’s aftermath, the Army said residents would need to hose down outdoor surfaces, vehicles, and play equipment in an effort to flush away any lead dust deposited during the detonation.
But experts have expressed doubt about how practical the safety guidance is.
At a news briefing, University of Iowa professor David Cwiertny, the director of the Center for Health Effects of Environmental Contamination, warned that long-term monitoring would be necessary to track the lead’s distribution.
“We know that, unlike a porch or patio table, you cannot simply wipe down farm fields, gardens or topsoil because those surfaces are hard to clean,” Cwiertny said.
“We will ultimately need to rely on actual field samples after the event to measure how much lead settles there and understand what it means for our land, those crops and the quality of the environment.”
The Army has yet to issue revised instructions or specify new evacuation hours following the delayed detonation.
Earthjustice lawyers like Chau say the lack of communication is part of the problem.
“The way they’ve gone about notifying people and claiming that they’re going to clean things up when they don’t even know the extent of impact, that is extremely concerning,” Chau told Al Jazeera.
US Representative Eric Sorensen, the only meteorologist serving in Congress, said the Army should be looking at a window of opportunity that presents the least potential for off-site exposure.
In a video posted on Thursday, Sorensen said, “The most optimum conditions for controlled detonation would be when we have an inversion of clouds, warm air over cool, with light winds.”
He warned that the National Weather Service’s forecast does not offer those favourable conditions over the coming week, and he questioned why the detonations…

Watch: Drone footage shows aftermath of deadly fire at Indonesian factory
At least three people have been killed after a fire at a confectionery factory in western Java on Saturday, with the death toll expected to rise.
Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for around 36 missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.
Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.
Rescuers recovered 24 body bags from the fire as of Sunday evening, as search operations continue to locate missing people.
Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire on Saturday evening.
The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km (31km) west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.
Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.
Local media reported that the search had been called off for the night late on Sunday, and would resume on Monday.
"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.
Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.
Firefighters had been called to the building at 16:30 local time (09:30 GMT) on Saturday - but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.
"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.
The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.
On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot on Sunday condemned arson attacks by settlers on Palestinian villages in the West Bank as “Jewish terrorism.” Israeli police said they opened an investigation into the attacks, which came nearly a month after an inconclusive election stripped incumbent Prime Minister ⁠Benjamin Netanyahu of his majority.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Israeli ​militant settlers attacked Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank early on Sunday, starting fires and scrawling racist graffiti, residents said, prompting an accusation of "Jewish terrorism" from the man trying to form an Israeli government.
The attacks, the latest in an escalation that began after Hamas launched attacks ​on Israel from ‌the Gaza Strip in 2023, come nearly a month after an inconclusive election stripped incumbent Prime Minister ⁠Benjamin Netanyahu of his majority.
Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.
Reuters saw burned-out Palestinian vehicles and walls spray-painted with slogans ‌such as "Revenge" and "Death to Arabs" in villages near Ramallah. No one immediately claimed responsibility and no injuries were ⁠reported.
Eisenkot called the attacks "Jewish terrorism", saying that "extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel's national security and foreign relations".
He said the policies of ​Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich , ultra-nationalist ministers in Netanyahu's cabinet, had "brought the area to the brink of anarchy, ‌and the authorities have yet to address the crisis".
Netanyahu has not yet commented but Foreign Minister Gideon Saar condemned the attacks by a "handful of extremists" and said they are "against our values and do not represent the law-abiding citizens of Judea and Samaria" — the biblical names for the West Bank.
"Israeli ‌authorities are firmly committed to enforcing the law against extremist violence," he told the ELNET Jerusalem Summit.
UN bodies and most countries of the world deny the legality of the ​settlements, which make the prospect of an independent Palestinian state ever more remote, a position Israel disputes.
Read more 'We see our culture being stolen': How Israeli settlers are attacking West Bank olive groves
Israeli police said they opened an investigation into the attacks, while the military condemned the violence, saying soldiers and police had been dispatched to the areas ​of Deir as-Sudan, Deir Abu Masha'al, Kafr Malik and At-Tuwani "following reports and footage showing vehicles being set on fire and graffiti being sprayed ​in the area".
Ben-Gvir replied in an X post that Eisenkot's condemnation amounted to selling out ​to Arab parties, which could become part of a possible new government. Smotrich favours settlement expansion and wants Israel to annex the West Bank.
Yousef Jabareen, head of the Joint List, the ​largest Arab party in Israel's parliament, said the attacks were "the direct result of the deepening occupation and a government policy under which violence against Palestinians has become an everyday occurrence", citing encouragement from Ben-Gvir and Smotrich.
Israel's parliament was sworn in on November 10 without a new government, after the election on October 27 stripped Netanyahu of his majority but left others with no clear path to power.
Read more Eisenkot invites Netanyahu’s party for ‘marathon’ Israeli coalition talks
President Isaac Herzog has ⁠tasked Eisenkot, who heads the centre-right Yashar, with forming a government, while Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister.
Unless Eisenkot forms a unity government with Netanyahu, he is likely to ⁠need support from Arab ​parties to be able to count on a majority of parliament's 120 seats.
If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.

Authorities in Java are searching for dozens of missing workers as they continue to battle remaining hotspots.
Indonesian authorities are set to resume the search for missing workers on Monday after police removed 24 body bags from a factory in Java gutted by a fire.
Firefighters continued to battle remaining hotspots on Sunday after the blaze broke out on Saturday evening at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia candy factory in Cikande, Serang regency, West Java province.
A search for dozens of missing workers was suspended overnight but would resume Monday morning, Hendra Kurniawan, the police chief of Indonesia’s Banten province, told local broadcaster Metro TV on Sunday.
Steven Erwin Wijaya, the CEO of the factory’s parent company, PT United Family Food, said at a news conference that about 300 people were present for Saturday’s shift, with 65 of them believed to have been in the affected area when the fire broke out.
In a statement that followed, the factory said 24 of the 65 workers had returned home, four were receiving medical treatment, 29 remained ‌missing, and the whereabouts of another eight had yet to be confirmed.
At a news conference on Sunday, Wahyu Hidayati Dwi Palupi, a police disaster victim identification official, said the intensity of the fire had made it impossible to identify the recovered victims visually. She said they would collect DNA samples from relatives and the personal belongings of the missing workers, a process that could take two to three weeks.
The number of dead was not immediately clear. Police said that one body bag could contain parts ⁠of more than one person.
Authorities said the cause of the fire was being investigated. Parts of the building remained at risk of collapse, an official added.
Photos and videos circulating online on Sunday showed flames and thick smoke coming from the factory, which borders the capital, Jakarta. Footage from inside the three-storey building appeared to show the fire caused extensive damage, with equipment blackened and destroyed.
Indonesia has suffered several deadly fires in recent years.
A fire in an office building in Jakarta killed at least 22 people last December. An explosion at an Indonesian nickel-processing plant killed at least 13 people in 2023.

Sunday’s dinner is the third private event for top holders of the $Trump meme coin, launched shortly before his second inauguration.
United States President Donald Trump will host a third private dinner for top investors in his meme coin $TRUMP, reigniting questions about potential conflicts of interest with his cryptocurrency ventures.
Sunday’s gala will take place at the Trump National Golf Club outside Washington, DC.
According to the dinner’s official website, the top 185 meme-coin holders will be invited to a gala dinner, where guests will include businessman Kevin O’Leary and boxer Floyd Mayweather.
The top 29 holders, meanwhile, will be given special access to a VIP reception where Trump will reportedly be present.
“There will be no private meetings with The President. No gifts will be accepted,” the website said of the VIP reception.
The event has been billed as “a once-in-a-lifetime experience — an evening you will talk about forever”.
But Democrats have accused the Republican leader of leveraging his public office for profit in violation of federal law. They see such dinners as an opportunity for private interests to pay for access to the president.
“Trump is continuing to exploit the presidency for his personal gain,” Kendall Witmer, the deputy communications director for the Democratic National Committee, said in a statement.
In October, shortly after the gala was announced, eight Democratic senators issued an open letter promising to investigate any conflicts of interest such an event might raise.
“President Trump’s continued monetization of his name and likeness once again raises serious ethical concerns, necessitating this request for a robust inquiry into the President’s financial entanglements and personal profiteering,” the letter said.
The Democratic Party has since won majorities in both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm race, paving the way for possible inquiries and subpoenas when the new members are sworn in next year.
Trump’s White House has dismissed the criticism, calling the dinner a “private event, not a government function”. It has also emphasised that “there is no promise of official government action in exchange for attending”.
Trump has also argued that many of his assets are held in a trust while he is in office, though that trust is largely run by his family members.
The president is a stakeholder in cryptocurrency firms like World Liberty Financial, and has made promoting cryptocurrency a central part of his second term.
Under his leadership, the US Treasury established a reserve of digital currency assets, as part of Trump’s effort to make the US the “crypto capital of the world”.
Sunday’s gala is believed to be the third such dinner for top $Trump meme coin holders.
Meme coins trade on a popular likeness from the internet. Trump launched his on January 17, 2025, days before the start of his second term.
To encourage meme-coin purchases, Trump and his business partners held private events on May 22, 2025, and again on April 25, 2026, for top holders of the cryptocurrency.
The first was held at the same Trump golf club outside Washington, DC, and the second took place at Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s Florida resort.
The May 2025 dinner reportedly required a minimum of $55,000 in $Trump coins to attend.
At the time, Chinese crypto investor Justin Sun was declared the winner of a “contest” for who held the most $TRUMP coins. Sun held about $18m of the coin in 2025, as well as tokens from World Liberty Financial.
Earlier this year, Sun sued World Liberty Financial , saying it had frozen his access to the assets he owned with it, making it impossible for him to sell them.
Trump’s inauguration in January 2025 proved a major boost for his coin, pushing its value to $74.
The $Trump coin has since lost value. On the eve of the gala dinner, it is worth about $0.88.
According to financial disclosure forms released earlier this year, Trump earned more than $2.2bn in 2025, the first year of his second term.
Much of that wealth came from meme coins, tokens and other digital assets. Some $636m came from $Trump meme coin sales.

Finland says work is continuing on the Sparta II ship on Sunday
A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.
The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.
It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.
The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.
Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.
The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Border Guard was responsible for the investigation into the attack and was co-operating with other relevant authorities.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

Schumer, who has led the Democratic caucus since 2017, faces a challenge from Chris Van Hollen in his bid to be the next Senate majority leader.
Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the United States Senate, is facing backlash against his bid to serve as Senate majority leader in the incoming Congress.
On Sunday, President ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Donald Trump added to the ongoing criticism of Schumer’s leadership, signalling there would be tension with the White House if Schumer were picked again to lead the Democratic caucus.
“It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Leader,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
“He failed badly as ‘Leader’ once before, one of the worst in history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again.”
The debate over Schumer’s leadership has underscored divides within the Democratic Party, particularly in the wake of the November 3 midterm elections.
Following a historic set of victories, Democrats are set to take control of both chambers of Congress in January.
Schumer, who leads the Democratic Senate minority, is hoping to retain his leadership position. A closed-door, secret-ballot vote is scheduled for December 1 to decide the majority leader.
A senator representing New York since 1999, Schumer has expressed confidence in his odds, saying he has the necessary votes to stay in charge.
“I will be elected majority leader,” Schumer told reporters last week.
But critics say Schumer, who will turn 76 on Monday, is ill-suited to lead a Senate Democratic caucus increasingly shaped by younger, anti-establishment lawmakers.
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, backed by progressives, has mounted a campaign to challenge Schumer for the majority leader role.
Van Hollen told NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday that he, too, was confident of winning.
“If you look at our caucus, you can see a huge appetite for change. They are seeing the American people and the Democratic Party calling for change. They also want to change the way we do business in the United States Democratic caucus and the United States Senate,” he said.
Schumer has also seen falling public approval ratings. In mid-November, a poll by the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos found that 34 percent of self-identified Democrats viewed Schumer favourably. That percentage was down from 38 percent in February.
November’s poll also suggested that 43 percent of Democrats held an unfavourable view of Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017.
The Senate Democratic leader is the only unresolved role among Congress’s top four positions.
House Democrats last week nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker in the next Congress.
Meanwhile, John Thune will continue to lead Senate Republicans, and Representative Jim Jordan ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌will succeed Speaker Mike Johnson as the top House Republican.

Virginia dinner comes as Democrats accuse president of improperly profiting from his cryptocurrency ventures
Donald Trump is scheduled to headline his third cryptocurrency gala on ⁠Sunday night at his ​country club in Virginia, rewarding top holders of his own meme coin as Democrats accuse the president of improperly profiting from his crypto ventures.
The dinner, set to take place at the Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, will include meet-and-greets with Trump supporters including the boxing champion Floyd Mayweather, Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary, NBA champion Tristan Thompson and mentalist Lior Suchard, according to the event’s website .
The gala’s access and perks are divided by tiers for the 185 holders of $TRUMP, the president’s meme coin. A Trump fragrance, a poster, a “commemorative” ticket, and a “Trump watch” are reserved for 120 attendees. Meanwhile, the top 29 investors are invited to a VIP reception, and the top four will receive a “TRUMP 18K Gold Watch”.
Trump has hosted two similar galas since he took office last year, bringing a flurry of criticism as Democrats accuse Trump and his family of monetizing his brand through an array of equities and crypto ventures while in office.
After sweepingwins in the midterms, Democrats have vowed to investigate conflicts of interest involving Trump and his personal wealth during his presidency. They also say they plan to push for legislation that would ban activities such as the meme coin gala dinner.
“This dinner and scoring mechanism appear carefully constructed to increase investment in $TRUMP, allowing the President to abuse the power of his office to personally enrich himself, as he has throughout this term,” reads a letter sent by Adam Schiff and eight other US senators last month.
Since returning to the White House, Trump has made more than $1bn from his crypto businesses , according to financial disclosures released in June. Trump received more than $500m from his World Liberty Financial business selling new crypto products, and raked another $600m from sales of souvenir-type “meme” coins stamped with Trump’s face. Trump launched his $Trump meme coin days before his inauguration.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Interest in the $TRUMP coin dinner has plummeted, with contestants’ combined holdings dropping from $148m in May 2025 to $8.6m in this month’s gala.
More than half of the digital wallets publicly listed on the contest leaderboard for Sunday’s dinner are tied directly to crypto exchanges that bar US-based users, indicating they ‌are linked to foreign nationals, according to an analysis of blockchain data prepared for Reuters by the nonpartisan, non-profit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.
“Neither the President nor his family ⁠has ever engaged — or will ever engage — in conflicts of interest,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Reuters ​earlier this year. “President Trump proudly made ​the United States the crypto capital of the world ​through executive actions.“
The Trump family ’s other crypto-connected equities and ventures have also fallen in value to record ​lows. Together, outside investors in their ‌five main crypto and ​crypto-linked projects have lost more than $5bn​, according to a Reuters analysis.
The Trump meme coin has earned the Trump family at least $635m, according to the president’s June financial disclosure statement . In total, the Trumps had earned at least $2.3bn through April from their four main crypto ventures, including the meme coin.
The president’s stake in a fifth crypto-linked venture, Trump Media & Technology Group, is worth about $430m.

Incident occurred near the end of Sunday night show by US rapper Don Toliver, with one person taken to hospital
Police have evacuated Manchester’s Co-op Live arena after a substance believed to be teargas was let off in the crowd during a Don Toliver concert.
Greater Manchester police said the incident occurred near the end of the US rapper’s show on Sunday evening.
Greater Manchester police said concertgoers had been safely evacuated, with several people being assessed on site for side effects as a precaution and inquiries under way to determine what the substance was. No serious injuries have been reported.
Assistant chief constable Steph Parker said in a statement: “Our priority was to ensure the safety of every person that was attending the concert.
“Several people were treated on site, and one has been taken to hospital at this time. Anyone who has left the event and since become unwell is advised to attend their local hospital.
“We understand the concern that this incident will have raised – particularly those with loved ones at the venue last night – and we’d like to thank everyone for their patience as we dealt with it.
“There were over 12,000 people in attendance during this concert who were safely escorted from the arena so they could make their way home.”
She continued: “Our declaration of a major incident has allowed us to ensure emergency services and partner agencies can work together quickly and effectively to coordinate a safe response.
“We will now begin to fully understand what this substance was and how this incident came about.”
The north-west ambulance service said one person was taken to hospital and more than 50 were assessed by clinicians.
The service said in a statement: “We deployed several emergency crews, including our Hazardous Area Response Team, to support the safe assessment and treatment of people at the scene.
“More than 50 people have been assessed by our clinicians, with some reporting eye and respiratory symptoms. Decontamination is being carried out as a precaution and one patient has been taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment.
“The incident remains ongoing and our teams remain at the scene assessing and caring for patients. We continue to work closely with emergency service partners while inquiries are carried out to establish what the substance was.
“Anyone at tonight’s event who has since noticed side effects or become ill should seek medical advice.”
Footage shared on social media appeared to show concertgoers coughing and covering their mouths as they left the venue.
Co-op Live has the capacity to hold 23,500 people, with American singer Phoebe Bridgers scheduled to perform at the venue on Thursday.
Don Toliver is partway through the UK leg of his Octane World Tour.
